overview.summary: Lawyers advise people and organizations about their legal rights and duties, prepare legal documents and represent clients in disputes or negotiations.
overview.problems: They help people understand the law, resolve disagreements and make agreements that protect their interests.
overview.worksWith: Clients, other lawyers, judges and court staff, and in companies, managers and business teams.
overview.workplaces: Law firms, courts, company legal departments, government bodies and non-profit organizations.

timeline.title: Reading and planning
timeline.description: The lawyer reads new emails and case notes, checks deadlines and decides which tasks come first.
timeline.why: Missing a legal deadline can seriously harm a client.

timeline.title: Legal research and drafting
timeline.description: The lawyer looks up laws and earlier cases, then drafts a document such as a contract, a notice or a court filing.
timeline.why: Arguments and documents must be accurate, clear and well supported.

timeline.title: Client meeting or call
timeline.description: The lawyer listens to the client's situation, explains the options in plain language and agrees the next steps.
timeline.why: Clients need to understand their choices to make good decisions.

timeline.title: Court, negotiation or meetings
timeline.description: Lawyers who work in disputes may attend hearings. Others negotiate terms or advise teams inside a company.
timeline.why: This is where preparation turns into results for the client.

timeline.title: Follow-up and records
timeline.description: The lawyer updates notes, sends documents and records the time spent on each matter.
timeline.why: Good records keep work organized and support billing.

timeline.title: Long hours before deadlines
timeline.description: Before a hearing or a deal closes, some lawyers work evenings or weekends.
timeline.why: Legal deadlines are fixed, and the work must be right.

responsibilities: Advising clients on their rights and options
Representing clients or negotiating on their behalf
Following professional ethics and court rules
challenges: Hours can be long and demanding, particularly in some firms.
Deadlines are strict and the stakes can be high.
Cases rarely end in a clear win for everyone involved.
Clients may be distressed or difficult to deal with.
The job involves a lot of reading and writing.
Strict ethical duties, such as confidentiality, always apply.
Competition for training places and jobs can be strong.
workEnvironment: Mostly office based, with visits to courts or clients. Law firms, courts, company legal teams and government bodies all differ. The day-to-day work depends heavily on the area of law, such as criminal, corporate, family or property.
rewards: Helping people deal with serious problems
Many areas of law to specialize in
Respect when you are trusted to give good advice
tradeoffs: Heavy workload and stress at busy times
Emotional weight in some kinds of cases
Income and conditions vary widely by country, employer and type of practice

activity.title: Read a simple contract and summarize it
steps: Find a short, public terms-and-conditions page, such as for a library card or a free online service.
Underline what the customer has to do and what the company has to do.
Write a one-page summary in plain language.
Note whether careful reading felt interesting or tiring.
activity.outcome: You practise careful reading and plain-language explanation, which are everyday legal skills.
activity.safety: This is a learning exercise only and is not legal advice. Do not accept or reject real agreements based on it, and ask a qualified lawyer about real legal matters.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
